consensus: Fine-tuning means taking a pretrained general model and training it further on task-, domain-, or style-specific examples.
The main purpose is to make a model more useful for a narrower production workflow when prompts alone are not enough.
Sources agree it can improve consistency, domain language, and repeated-task behavior, especially in operational settings.
It is presented as cheaper and faster than training a model from scratch, but it still requires curated data and evaluation.

evidence_quality: Moderate: two sources agree on the core definition and practical role.
The evidence is mostly explanatory rather than experimental; it gives useful framing but not measured results.
One source includes a rhetorical claim that fine-tuning is a 'weekend project now,' but this is not substantiated here and should be treated as a lightweight aside, not a general fact.
executive_synthesis: Fine-tuning is the process of adapting a pretrained model to a narrower task, domain, or style by training it further on specialized examples. In the reviewed sources, it is framed as a practical production technique for cases where a general model is useful but not specific enough: it can improve consistency, domain language, policy adherence, and repeated workflow performance, while reducing reliance on long prompts. The tradeoff is that it adds data curation, training, evaluation, and ongoing maintenance, so it is most justified when the same task repeats often enough to repay that setup cost.
practical_takeaway: Treat fine-tuning as an operational optimization for recurring, narrow workflows: use it when you have enough domain examples and a clear success criterion, and avoid assuming it is worthwhile unless the performance gain justifies the extra data and maintenance work.
tensions: The sources agree on the definition and use cases, but one source adds a casual claim that fine-tuning is now a 'weekend project'; this is not corroborated by the rest of the evidence.
The sources imply strong practical value in production, but they do not provide measurements, so the size of the benefit remains uncertain.
title: Fine-tuning
what_to_remember: Fine-tuning = further training a pretrained model on specialized examples.
It is mainly useful for narrow, repeated tasks where prompts alone are not enough.
It can improve consistency, style, and domain-specific behavior.
It is usually cheaper than training from scratch, but not free: it needs curated data and evaluation.
The key question is whether the workflow gains outweigh the added setup and maintenance.
